explanations.explanation: That's the one. The LORD asks, "Can a woman forget her nursing child, or lack compassion for the son of her womb?" (Isaiah 49:15). A mother forgetting her nursing child is hard to picture. Then He says that even if she could forget, He will not forget Zion.

Nice try, friend, but a house isn't what the LORD picks. He asks about a woman and "…her nursing child…" and the question is about compassion for "…the son of her womb?" (Isaiah 49:15). A person is a lot harder to forget than an address. Even then, He says, "…I will not forget you!"

I get why you'd pick it, but her name never comes up. The LORD asks, "Can a woman forget her nursing child, or lack compassion for the son of her womb?" (Isaiah 49:15). The question is about a child, not a name. Then He says He won't forget Zion even if she could.

Yes, and listen to how He says it. "Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!" (Isaiah 49:15). Zion had just said she was forgotten, and this answers her straight to her face. Nothing is left hanging, friend.

This one is true, and the text says it plainly. The LORD says, "Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!" (Isaiah 49:15). He starts with a mother, the hardest person to picture forgetting, and then goes even further than that. Zion said she'd been forgotten, and He tells her otherwise.

Walls it is. The LORD says, "Behold, I have inscribed you on the palms of My hands; your walls are ever before Me." (Isaiah 49:16). Zion's walls are right there in front of Him all the time. Zion thought she was forgotten, and here she is written on His palms.

Gates is a fair guess for a city, friend, but that's not the word here. The text says, "your walls are ever before Me." (Isaiah 49:16). Zion is written on His palms, and her walls stay in front of Him. I'd say that's a pretty close look at her.

Towers would look great on a city, but the verse says walls. "…I have inscribed you on the palms of My hands; your walls are ever before Me." (Isaiah 49:16). Zion said she was forgotten, and here He has her written on His own hands. Walls, always in view.

Builders, yes, friend! The verse says, "Your builders hasten back; your destroyers and wreckers depart from you." (Isaiah 49:17). The ones who tear down are leaving. The ones who rebuild are in a hurry to get back. That's a big change for Zion in one verse.

Soldiers aren't named here. The verse says, "Your builders hasten back; your destroyers and wreckers depart from you." (Isaiah 49:17). The ones hurrying back are the builders, which is good news for a city that's been torn up. Wreckers go out, builders come in.

Priests are a sensible guess, but the verse names someone else. "Your builders hasten back; your destroyers and wreckers depart from you." (Isaiah 49:17). Builders are the ones hurrying back. After all that wrecking, a city needs somebody with tools.

A bride is right. The LORD says, "you will wear them all as jewelry and put them on like a bride." (Isaiah 49:18). Zion thought she'd been forgotten, and now she's dressed up in a gathering crowd. It's about as far from forgotten as you can get, friend.

A mourner is not it, and I'm glad, because this verse turns the other way. The LORD says Zion will "…put them on like a bride." (Isaiah 49:18). That's a picture of celebration, with the crowd gathering to her like jewelry. Zion started out saying she was forgotten, and now she's dressed up.

Not a soldier, friend. The LORD says, "you will wear them all as jewelry and put them on like a bride." (Isaiah 49:18). Nothing in the picture is about a battle, because a bride dressed in her jewelry is a celebration. The crowd coming her way is something she gets to wear.

Careful, this one's the other way around. The LORD says her ruined places and ravaged land "…will now indeed be too small for your people…" (Isaiah 49:19). So there will be more people than room, not extra room. It's a crowded problem, and the good kind.

Right, it's false. The LORD says her ruined and desolate places and ravaged land "…will now indeed be too small for your people…" (Isaiah 49:19). Instead of empty space, there are more people than room. Her ruins are about to be packed.

That's it. Zion says, "Who has begotten these for me?" and then, "Look, I was left all alone, so where did they come from?" (Isaiah 49:21). She's looking at a crowd of children she didn't see coming. I'd say she's stunned, and I don't blame her.

She isn't asking about leaving, friend. She asks, "…I was left all alone, so where did they come from?" (Isaiah 49:21). Nobody is heading for the door in this verse. They've shown up, and she's asking how.

That's a fair guess, but Zion doesn't complain about timing. She asks, "Who has begotten these for me?" and "Look, I was left all alone, so where did they come from?" (Isaiah 49:21). Her question is about where they came from. I think she's too surprised to be picky about the schedule.

Yes, they carry them to her. The Lord GOD says, "They will bring your sons in their arms and carry your daughters on their shoulders." (Isaiah 49:22). He lifts His hand and raises His banner to the nations, and the sons are brought in arms while the daughters are carried on shoulders. That's a gentle way to travel, friend.

No servants here. The Lord GOD says the nations "…will bring your sons in their arms and carry your daughters on their shoulders." (Isaiah 49:22). Being carried in arms and on shoulders is how you'd treat someone you're looking after. They're bringing them to Zion.

It's the opposite direction. The Lord GOD says, "They will bring your sons in their arms and carry your daughters on their shoulders." (Isaiah 49:22). The nations bring them toward Zion, not away from her. Arms for the sons, shoulders for the daughters.

Fathers, that's right. The LORD says, "Kings will be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers." (Isaiah 49:23). Kings are her foster fathers and queens are her nursing mothers. That's quite a household for Zion.

Brothers would be a nice family word, but the verse uses a different one. "Kings will be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers." (Isaiah 49:23). Fathers and mothers, which are the ones who raise a child. The kings and queens do the caring.
Masters sounds like a boss, friend, and that's not the word. Here the kings are called foster fathers (Isaiah 49:23). Their queens are called nursing mothers. Not a boss in sight.

explanations.answer: They will never be put to shame
explanations.explanation: That's the promise. The LORD says Zion will know that He is the LORD. Then comes the promise: "those who hope in Me will never be put to shame." (Isaiah 49:23). Hope placed in Him doesn't end in shame.

That sounds nice, but it isn't what He says. The LORD says, "those who hope in Me will never be put to shame." (Isaiah 49:23). Zion had plenty of trouble in this very passage. The promise is that hoping in Him won't end in shame.

explanations.answer: They will never have to wait
explanations.explanation: I wish I could say that, friend, because waiting is hard. But the LORD says, "those who hope in Me will never be put to shame." (Isaiah 49:23). Hope in this verse is about the outcome, not about skipping the wait. Hoping in Him doesn't end in shame.

True. Verse 24 asks, "Can the plunder be snatched from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be delivered?" Then the LORD says, "Even the captives of the mighty will be taken away, and the plunder of the tyrant will be retrieved…" (Isaiah 49:25). That question sounds like a hard one. The answer given is yes, they will be taken away.

It's actually true, friend. Look at what the LORD says in verse 25: "Even the captives of the mighty will be taken away, and the plunder of the tyrant will be retrieved…" (Isaiah 49:25). Those are His words, so the statement on the card matches them. The captives are taken away from the mighty.

Yes, that's who. The LORD says, "I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children." (Isaiah 49:25). Those who contend with Zion are the ones He contends with. Zion isn't left to handle them alone.

Not the builders, friend. In verse 17 they hasten back to her, and that's a different thing from what the LORD says here. He says, "I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children." (Isaiah 49:25). He contends with those who contend with Zion.

The nations show up in verse 22, bringing her sons. The Lord GOD says, "They will bring your sons in their arms…" (Isaiah 49:22). Then the LORD says, "I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children." (Isaiah 49:25). So it's the ones who contend with her.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, "Then all mankind will know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob." (Isaiah 49:26). That's all mankind, not only Zion. So the word "only" is what breaks this one.

Right, it's false. The LORD says, "Then all mankind will know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob." (Isaiah 49:26). The knowing reaches past Zion to all mankind. That's a much bigger audience than one city.
